source.title: Separating the Effects of Batch Normalization on CNN Training Speed and Stability Using Classical Adaptive Filter Theory
source.authors: Elaina Chai; Mert Pilanci; B. Murmann

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares normalization and initialization variants during CNN training and reports training-curve and stability outcomes relevant to V3 and V6, but it does not reproduce the original studies' methods exactly.
record.gate_note: The reported training curves use validation error, not training classification error. Eigenvalue and variance measurements are not rows because they do not measure the behavior named by these claim versions. Figure values are not numerically stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The study compares BatchNorm with unnormalized networks and reports convergence speed and learning-rate tolerance on MNIST and CIFAR-10, directly testing V6. It does not measure depth-dependent training error or test the complete Fixup recipe required for V3.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate but understates the distinction between architectures. The authors conclude that LeNet experiments support separate low-learning-rate speed and high-learning-rate stability mechanisms. ResNet experiments support the stability mechanism, but standard BatchNorm fails to match selective amplification at low learning rates, leaving its speed mechanism unresolved. BatchNorm before convolution most closely approximates NLMS and shows similar gradient-noise suppression.
record.recipe_differences: Compares BatchNorm and related normalization variants during CNN training, including a FixupCore initialization condition; uses validation-error curves and stability observations rather than measuring training classification error as in V1.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior varies with learning rate, architecture and normalization variant. At high µ on MNIST, BatchNorm resembles BN Suppress; at low µ on CIFAR-10 ResNet20, BN Amplify FixupCore trains fastest and standard BatchNorm does not match it.

fits_no_version.finding: BN Amplify FixupCore converges fastest at low learning rates and outperforms standard BatchNorm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selective channel amplification combined with FixupCore can outperform standard BatchNorm in low-learning-rate ResNet20 training.

fits_no_version.finding: With a frozen fully connected layer, BatchNorm after convolution lowers accuracy from 99% to 95%; BatchNorm before convolution and NLMS suppress injected gradient noise more effectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization placement affects gradient-noise sensitivity and final accuracy when the classifier is frozen. These outcomes alone do not establish accuracy gain per epoch or learning-rate tolerance.

record.peer_reviewed: Asilomar Conference on Signals, Systems and Computers, 2020
record.problems: The relevant training outcomes are validation error rather than training classification error. Curves are figure-only without numerical values. In the ResNet20 stability discussion, the text does not identify which two plotted variants are the networks that become unstable.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on V3 or V6 were omitted. Eigenvalue and variance plots were excluded because they measure intermediate quantities, not the training behavior named by these versions.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error, random labels, capacity dependence, and regularization or early-stopping effects.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious minima, and extra-width effects.
Depth-dependent training error in matched plain and residual networks, deep plain tanh initialization, and the complete Fixup recipe.

Activation-matched initialization effects on learning speed and trainable depth, Gaussian versus orthogonal weights, and extremely deep convolutional networks. Initial variance and eigenvalue measurements alone do not establish these outcomes.
Recovery above the initial linearized stability threshold, catapult dynamics, and full-batch edge-of-stability behavior.

The original sigmoid MNIST, VGG, and Inception configurations; complete Fixup with its scalar biases and multipliers; and a readable matched BatchNorm-versus-unnormalized speed comparison for ResNet20 at low learning rates.

missing.what: A condition-specific BatchNorm stability comparator for R6 at learning rate 0.05, replacing R4's undifferentiated learning-rate sweep.

The additional low-learning-rate MNIST convergence comparison at learning rate 0.1 and the stated eventual equality of validation error for all networks below 0.5, separating speed from final accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: Validation-error trajectories can test V6's accuracy-speed claim, although they cannot establish V1 or V3's training-error claims. Neither outperforming BatchNorm with a novel method nor instability under an incomplete Fixup recipe justifies the record's proposed scope limitations.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100 training classification error, corrupted or random labels, model size, or early stopping.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student problem or width sweep is tested.

The ResNet20 experiments use FixupCore, described as the core portion of Fixup, rather than testing the full Fixup recipe. The study does not compare plain and shortcut networks at matched depths or test ImageNet.
The experiments do not compare the initialization methods or trainable depths named in this version.
The study does not test the learning-rate stability threshold or the catapult and edge-of-stability dynamics in this version.
The study tests LeNet-like networks on MNIST and ResNet20 on CIFAR-10, but not VGG on CIFAR-10 or Inception on ImageNet. Its no-normalization residual condition uses FixupCore.

rows.check: FixupCore is an unnormalized comparator for BatchNorm's stability benefit, not a test of complete Fixup or depth degradation.
